questions.stem:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of 1 MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size 4 KB. The virtual address space is 64 GB and physical address space is 1 GB. If each TLB entry stores a 4-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a 2-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ________. (answer in integer)

Note: $1\text{K} = 2^{10}$, $1\text{M} = 2^{20}$, $1\text{G} = 2^{30}$

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: Virtual memory is cut into pages and physical memory into frames of the same size. A virtual address is a page number followed by an offset inside the page; a physical address is a frame number followed by the same offset. The page table, which maps page numbers to frame numbers, sits in main memory, so reading it on every access would double the cost. The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small hardware table that keeps recent translations. One TLB entry holds one translation: the page number, the frame number, and extra bits, here a process id (so two processes that use the same page number are not confused) and control bits. Because an entry covers one page, the TLB reach, the memory the entries cover together, is the number of entries times the page size. The rule: entries = reach / page size, entry width = sum of its fields, and TLB size = entries × entry width. A page number has (address bits − offset bits) bits, and the offset has $\log_2$(page size) bits.

steps.title: Number of entries from the reach
steps.body: Each TLB entry maps one page, so the reach is the number of entries times the page size. The number of entries is $1\text{ MB} / 4\text{ KB} = 2^{20}/2^{12} = 2^8 = 256$.

steps.title: Widths of the page number and the frame number
steps.body: A 4 KB page needs a 12-bit offset. The virtual address space is $64\text{ GB} = 2^{36}$ bytes, so a page number has $36 - 12 = 24$ bits. Physical memory is $1\text{ GB} = 2^{30}$ bytes, so a frame number has $30 - 12 = 18$ bits. This is the chapter's formula for offset, VPN and PFN bits.

steps.title: Width of one entry
steps.body: An entry holds the 4-bit process id, the 24-bit page number, the 18-bit frame number and the 2-bit control field: 48 bits, exactly 6 bytes, so no rounding question arises.

steps.title: Size of the TLB
steps.body: Size = entries × entry width = $256 \times 6 = 1536$ bytes.

shortcut.body: Entries $= 2^{20-12} = 2^8$. Entry bits $= 4 + (36 - 12) + (30 - 12) + 2 = 48$, which is 6 bytes. Size $= 2^8 \times 6 = 1536$. Had the bits not summed to a multiple of 8, the question would have to say how to round; here it does not matter.

traps.text: Counting entries from the address space builds a page table, not a TLB: one entry per virtual page ($2^{24}$) or per frame ($2^{18}$). The reach fixes the TLB at 256 entries.
Dropping a field: without the process id an entry has 44 bits and the TLB 1408 bytes; without the control field, 46 bits and 1472 bytes; with only the page and frame numbers, 42 bits and 1344 bytes.
Giving the frame number the virtual width, 24 bits, makes the entry 54 bits and the TLB 1728 bytes. A frame number indexes physical memory, so it has 18 bits.

recognize.clues: The question gives a TLB reach, a page size and both address-space sizes, then asks for the TLB size in bytes with extra per-entry fields (process id, control bits).
recognize.contrast: Page table size counts one entry per virtual page of the whole address space; the TLB holds only reach divided by page size entries, and each entry stores the page number as well.

check.body: Check the entry count by working forward: 256 entries of 4 KB pages cover 256 x 4 KB = 1 MB, which is the stated reach. Check the width by the bit budget: 4 + 24 + 18 + 2 = 48, a whole number of bytes, so no rounding assumption was needed.

variation.stem: A TLB has a reach of 4 MB. Pages are 8 KB, the virtual address space is 32 GB and the physical address space is 512 MB. Each TLB entry stores a 6-bit process id, the page number, the frame number and a 4-bit control field. The size of the TLB in bytes is ________. (answer in integer)

questions.stem:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are 8 holes in the memory of sizes 20 KB, 4 KB, 25 KB, 18 KB, 7 KB, 9 KB, 15 KB, and 12 KB. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes P1 of size 16 KB and P2 of size 9 KB arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to P1 and P2, the number of holes of size less than 8 KB is ________. (answer in integer)

Note: $1\text{K} = 2^{10}$

steps.title: Best fit for P1
steps.body:
Best fit puts a request into the smallest hole that is at least as large as the request. For P1 (16 KB) the holes that fit are 20, 25 and 18 KB, and the smallest is 18 KB. P1 goes there and leaves a 2 KB hole.
Holes: 20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 9, 15, 12 KB.

steps.title: Best fit for P2
steps.body:
For P2 (9 KB) the holes that fit are 20, 25, 9, 15 and 12 KB, and the smallest is the 9 KB hole. It is an exact fit, so that hole disappears.
Holes: 20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 15, 12 KB.

steps.title: Count the holes below 8 KB
steps.body: The holes below 8 KB are 4, 2 and 7 KB, so the answer is 3. The 2 KB remainder cannot merge with another hole, because the 18 KB hole it came from had no hole beside it.

shortcut.body: Only two placements matter: 16 into 18 leaves 2, and 9 into 9 leaves nothing. Add the new 2 KB hole to the 4 and 7 KB holes already there: 3. First fit happens to give 3 on this list as well (it leaves 4 and 16), so a matching number does not prove the rule was applied correctly.

traps.text: Counting the exact fit as a 0 KB hole gives 4. P2 fills the 9 KB hole completely, so no hole remains there.
Worst fit (P1 into 25 KB, P2 into 20 KB) leaves 9 and 11 KB holes and gives 2, and counting the small holes before any allocation also gives 2 (the 4 and 7 KB holes).

recognize.clues: The wording names variable partitioning, a list of holes with sizes, requests arriving in order and the best-fit technique, then asks about the holes left.
recognize.contrast: First fit takes the first hole that is large enough and worst fit the largest. Best fit needs the whole list scanned for the smallest adequate hole, so the three can leave different leftovers.

check.body: Total free space must drop by exactly the memory handed out. The holes sum to 110 KB at the start and 85 KB at the end, and 16 + 9 = 25, so the arithmetic is consistent.

questions.stem:
Consider a demand paging system with three frames, and the following page reference string: 1 2 3 4 5 4 1 6 4 5 1 3 2. The contents of the frames are as follows initially and after each reference (from left to right):

The *-marked references cause page replacements.

Which one or more of the following could be the page replacement policy/policies in use?
options: Least Recently Used page replacement policy
Least Frequently Used page replacement policy
Most Frequently Used page replacement policy
Optimal page replacement policy

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: Demand paging loads a page into a frame only when it is referenced. A reference to a page that sits in no frame is a page fault. With a free frame the page simply goes in; with all three frames full, the replacement policy picks a victim page to throw out. The starred references in the table are the faults. The four policies differ only in how they pick the victim. LRU (least recently used) evicts the resident page whose last use is oldest. LFU (least frequently used) evicts the resident page with the fewest uses so far. MFU (most frequently used) evicts the one with the most uses so far, on the idea that a page used often has had its turn. OPT (optimal) evicts the resident page whose next use is farthest in the future, or that is never used again. LFU and MFU need a tie-break when counts are equal; the usual one is to evict the page loaded earliest. The rule: a policy can be the one in use only if every eviction in the table is a choice that policy could make.

steps.title: Read the victims off the table
steps.body: A replacement shows as a frame whose page changes. References 1, 2 and 3 fill empty frames. After that, the 4th reference (page 4) evicts 2, the 5th (page 5) evicts 3, the 8th (page 6) evicts 1, the 11th (page 1) evicts 4, the 12th (page 3) evicts 5 and the 13th (page 2) evicts 6. A policy is possible only if it can make all six of these choices.

steps.title: LRU and LFU are ruled out
steps.body: At the 4th reference the frames hold 1, 2 and 3, each used once, and page 1 is the least recently used, so LRU evicts 1, not 2. LFU counts uses: at the 8th reference page 1 has been used twice (references 1 and 7), page 4 twice (4 and 6) and page 5 once (5). LFU must evict 5, but the table evicts 1, so LFU fails whatever its tie-break.

steps.title: MFU is ruled out under the standard tie-breaks
steps.body: At the 4th reference pages 1, 2 and 3 all have count 1, so MFU must break a tie. Oldest first, the usual rule, evicts 1; newest first evicts 3. Page 2 is the middle page by load order, by recency and by number, so neither of those rules, nor ordering by page number, picks it. With counts kept across reloads MFU fails again at the 12th reference, where page 1 has three uses and the table evicts 5. MFU fits only if every tie happens to go the table's way and counts restart on reload, so it is rejected.

steps.title: OPT makes every choice
steps.body: OPT evicts the resident page whose next use is farthest away. At the 4th, 5th and 8th references the farthest page is unique and is the one the table evicts. From the 11th reference on, no resident page is used again, so every victim is optimal, and the table's victims (4, 5, 6) are the oldest-loaded pages each time. The answer is D only.

shortcut.body: Test the 4th reference first. OPT must evict 2, the page whose next use comes last (reference 13), while LRU evicts 1, and so do LFU and MFU under an oldest-first tie-break. That column alone leaves only D. To rule out LFU without any tie-break assumption, use the 8th reference: page 5 has the fewest uses, yet the table evicts page 1.

traps.text: MFU looks possible because the table is full of ties. Breaking ties by age or by page number, it evicts 1 or 3 at the 4th reference, never 2, and with counts kept across reloads it must evict 1 at the 12th. It matches only if each tie happens to go the table's way, and the official key lists D alone.
LFU survives the 4th and 5th references if ties are broken freely, but at the 8th reference page 5 has one use against two each for pages 1 and 4, and the table evicts page 1.
LRU fails at the first replacement: at the 4th reference page 1 was used longest ago (reference 1), and the table evicts page 2.
Rejecting OPT because the last three victims look arbitrary. When no resident page is used again, every victim is optimal, so those choices are valid OPT choices.

recognize.clues: The frame contents are given after each reference with replacement stars, and the task is to infer which policies could have produced them.
recognize.contrast: Predicting faults for a known policy is a simulation; here the direction is reversed, so each observed victim is tested against every policy. Ties in LFU and MFU need a stated tie-break.

check.body: Count the starred columns: the table has 9 faults, six first-time loads of pages 1 to 6 plus three reloads. Now run optimal on the string, choosing each victim by next use alone, and count its faults. It also gives 9, and no policy can do better than optimal. Separately, LRU would have evicted page 1 at the 4th reference, which the table does not do.

questions.stem:
A computer system supports a logical address space of $2^{32}$ bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into a $b$-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of $b$ is ________. (Answer in integer)

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: A page is a fixed-size block of the address space, here 4096 bytes. The offset is the position of a byte inside its page; a page of $2^k$ bytes needs a $k$-bit offset. A page table entry is one record, here 8 bytes, that maps one page to a frame, or in the outer table to a page of the inner table. An index is the number of the entry chosen in a table. Two-level paging stores the page table as a tree: the outer page table is indexed first and points to pages of the inner page table, an inner entry gives the frame, and the offset then picks the byte. Every table is stored in ordinary pages, so one page of a table holds $P/e$ entries, with $P$ the page size and $e$ the entry size, and an index into it needs $\log_2(P/e)$ bits. The rule: the three fields add up to the address width, the offset takes $\log_2 P$ bits, the inner index takes $\log_2(P/e)$ bits, and the outer index takes what is left.

steps.title: Offset within the desired page
steps.body: A page of $4096 = 2^{12}$ bytes needs a 12-bit offset.

steps.title: Index within a page of the inner table
steps.body: A page of the inner page table is an ordinary page of 4096 bytes, so it holds $4096/8 = 512 = 2^9$ entries of 8 bytes. The middle field selects one of them and has 9 bits. This is the chapter's rule that each level resolves $\log_2(P/e)$ bits (derivation: hierarchical page tables).

steps.title: The outer index takes the remaining bits
steps.body: The three fields fill the 32-bit address, so $b + 9 + 12 = 32$ and $b = 11$. The outer table then has $2^{11}$ entries, which fill four pages if they are also 8 bytes wide. The question ties only the inner table to the page size, so this is allowed.

shortcut.body: Bits per inner level $= \log_2(P/e) = 12 - 3 = 9$. The outer index gets what is left: $32 - 12 - 9 = 11$.

traps.text: Assuming 4-byte entries out of habit gives $\log_2(4096/4) = 10$ inner bits and $b = 10$. The question says eight bytes.
Splitting the 20 page-number bits evenly, 10 and 10, also gives 10. The split is set by how many 8-byte entries fit in a page, not by symmetry.
Answering 9, the width of the inner index, instead of the outer index $b$.

recognize.clues: The question says two-level hierarchical paging, gives the page size and the inner table entry size, and states that all pages have the same size, which fixes the inner index width.
recognize.contrast: In a single-level table the page number is all of the leftover bits. With two levels the inner index width is set by the page size and entry size, and only the outer index takes what remains.

check.body: Substitute $b=11$ and compare sizes. The outer table has $2^{11}$ entries of 8 bytes, which is $16384$ bytes, exactly 4 pages. The address space is then $2^{11}\cdot 2^{9}\cdot 2^{12}=2^{32}$ bytes, as given.

questions.stem: Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: A logical address is the address a program issues; a physical address names a location in main memory. Memory is cut into pages (logical) and frames (physical) of the same size, here 2048 bytes. Byte-addressable means each address names one byte. The offset is the byte's position inside its page, so a page of $2^k$ bytes needs $k$ offset bits, and the remaining high bits of the logical address are the page number. The page table has one entry per page number; each entry maps a page to a frame. The rule: the number of page table entries is $2^{\text{logical address bits} - \text{offset bits}}$.

steps.title: Offset width
steps.body: Byte-addressable memory with 2048-byte pages needs an offset of $\log_2 2048 = 11$ bits.

steps.title: One entry per virtual page
steps.body: A single-level page table has one entry for every page of the logical address space. The logical address leaves $32 - 11 = 21$ bits for the page number, so the table has $2^{21}$ entries: option A. The 20-bit physical address sets the width of each entry (a 9-bit frame number), not the number of entries.

shortcut.body: Entries $= 2^{\text{logical bits} - \text{offset bits}} = 2^{32 - 11}$. The physical width only sizes each entry, so ignore it.

traps.text: $2^{20}$ is the familiar answer for 32-bit addresses with 4 KB pages, and it is also the 20-bit physical width read as an exponent. Here the pages are 2 KB, so the offset is 11 bits.
$2^{22}$ follows from a 10-bit offset, that is, from taking the pages as 1 KB.
Counting frames, $2^{20 - 11} = 2^9$, gives the size of an inverted page table, which has one entry per frame; it is not offered.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the maximum number of entries of the page table and gives a logical address width, a physical address width and a page size.
recognize.contrast: The number of entries comes from the logical address; the physical address width only decides how many bits each entry needs for the frame number. Mixing them gives the number of frames instead.

check.body: Multiply back: the number of entries times the page size must equal the whole logical address space. Check that the exponent of the entry count plus 11 equals 32.

questions.stem:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:

The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.

A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:

1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.

If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page faults that will occur during execution of the process is ________. (Answer in integer)

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: A frame is a slot of main memory that holds one page, and here there are three, so at most three pages are resident. A reference to a resident page is a hit. A reference to any other page is a page fault: the page must be loaded, into an empty frame if there is one, otherwise in place of a victim page chosen by the replacement policy. Optimal (OPT) replacement evicts the resident page whose next use is farthest away, which needs the whole future string. In the modified version the OS sees only a window of four references at a fault: the current one and the next three. The rule: evict a resident page that does not occur in the window; if every resident page occurs in it, evict the one whose first occurrence in the window comes last.

steps.title: Simulate with three frames
steps.body: 1, 3 and 2 fault into empty frames. Page 4 faults with window 4, 2, 3, 1: pages 2 and 3 return first, page 1 last, so 1 is evicted. Pages 2 and 3 hit. Page 1 faults with window 1, 2, 4, 3: page 3 returns last, so 3 is evicted. Pages 2 and 4 hit. Page 3 faults with window 3, 1, 4, where the string ends; page 2 does not occur, so 2 is evicted. Pages 1 and 4 hit.

steps.title: Count the faults
steps.body: Faults occur at references 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 10: 6 page faults, 3 compulsory and 3 replacements. Every victim here is also the one full OPT would choose, so the count equals OPT's (derivation: optimal replacement is optimal, which counts faults as compulsory plus replacements).

shortcut.body: Trace only the faults, since a hit needs no decision. After the 3 compulsory faults, read each victim off the next three references: at the 4th reference evict 1 (window 4, 2, 3, 1), at the 7th evict 3 (window 1, 2, 4, 3), and at the 10th evict 2, which is missing from the window 3, 1, 4. That makes 3 + 3 = 6. The method is unsafe if two resident pages are both missing from a window, because the rule then does not fix the victim; that never happens on this string.

traps.text: Counting only the replacements gives 3. The question asks for page faults, and the first three references fault on empty frames.
Running LRU instead gives 8 faults; the policy looks ahead in the string, not back. FIFO gives 6 on this string by coincidence, so a match with FIFO does not confirm the method.

recognize.clues: The question defines a modified optimal algorithm that sees only the next four references including the current one, and asks for the fault count over a short string with three empty frames.
recognize.contrast: Full optimal looks at the entire remaining string; a limited window can leave two pages equally invisible, so the rule may need a tie-break. LRU looks backwards instead of forwards.

check.body: Run the same string under full optimal replacement, which sees the whole future and so is a lower bound for any limited window. It also gives 6 faults, and no policy can beat it, so 6 cannot be too high by a wrong eviction. The 3 compulsory faults plus 3 replacements agree with it.

questions.stem: Which of the following tasks is/are the responsibility/responsibilities of the memory management unit (MMU) in a system with paging-based memory management?
options: Allocate a new page table for a newly created process
Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table
Raise a trap when a virtual address is not found in the page table
Raise a trap when a process tries to write to a page marked with read-only permission in the page table

steps.title: Hardware versus software
steps.body: The MMU is hardware on the path of every memory access. It reads the page table that the OS built, through the page-table base register, and allocates nothing. Allocating and filling a page table for a new process is kernel code run at process creation, so A is not an MMU task.

steps.title: Translation and the two traps
steps.body: B: translation is the MMU's main job. It splits the address into page number and offset, finds the frame (TLB first, then the page table) and forms frame × page size + offset. C: if the entry is not valid, the MMU cannot translate and raises a page-fault trap; the OS handler then loads the page or ends the process. D: the protection bits sit in the same entry, and the MMU checks them on every access, trapping a write to a read-only page. The answer is B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Ask of each task whether it has to happen on every memory access, at hardware speed. Translating and checking the entry (valid bit, permission bits) does; allocating a table happens once per process and is done in software.

traps.text: A sounds like memory management, but the MMU only uses page tables. The OS allocates them, from its own list of free frames.
C gets left out because the OS handles page faults. Handling is the OS's job; detecting the invalid entry and raising the trap is the MMU's.
D gets left out by those who think protection is checked in software. The check runs in hardware on every access, which is what makes read-only code pages and copy-on-write work.

recognize.clues: The question asks which tasks belong to the MMU in a paging system, with options about building a table, translating addresses and raising traps on invalid or protected pages.
recognize.contrast: The kernel creates and edits page tables and services the trap; the MMU only reads the table and raises the trap. Mixing up who builds and who uses the table is the usual error.

check.body: Test the split with a second route: picture a processor that has only the MMU and no kernel running. Translating an address, trapping on an invalid entry and trapping on a write to a read-only page can all be done from the table alone, with no decision to make. Allocating a new table needs a free-frame list and a choice of frame, which are kernel data and kernel decisions the MMU has no access to, so A fails and B, C and D pass.

questions.stem:
Consider a 32-bit system with 4 KB page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes each. Assume 1 KB = $2^{10}$ bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory management, with the page table containing an outer page directory and an inner page table. The OS allocates a page for the outer page directory upon process creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page table, i.e., a page of the inner page table is allocated only if it contains at least one valid page table entry.

An active process in this system accesses 2000 unique pages during its execution, and none of the pages are swapped out to disk. After it completes the page accesses, let X denote the minimum and Y denote the maximum number of pages across the two levels of the page table of the process.

The value of X+Y is ________

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: A page is a 4 KB block of the address space, and a page table entry (PTE) is the 4-byte record that maps one page to a frame. An entry is valid when it holds a real mapping. A two-level page table is a tree: the outer page directory is one page of entries, each pointing to an inner page table, and an inner page table is a page of PTEs that map the process's pages. The directory is allocated when the process is created, so it always counts as one page. An inner page is allocated only when at least one of its entries is valid. The rule: the pages of page table = 1 + the number of inner pages that hold at least one valid entry. X takes the arrangement of the 2000 accessed pages that needs the fewest inner pages, and Y the arrangement that needs the most.

steps.title: Split the address
steps.body: A 4 KB page holds $4096/4 = 1024 = 2^{10}$ entries, so each level resolves 10 bits: a 10-bit directory index, a 10-bit inner index and a 12-bit offset. One inner page maps 1024 consecutive virtual pages, and the one-page directory has 1024 entries, so at most 1024 inner pages can exist.

steps.title: Minimum X: pack the pages
steps.body: Put the 2000 pages consecutively from the start of a 1024-page region. They need $\lceil 2000/1024 \rceil = 2$ inner pages, so with the directory $X = 1 + 2 = 3$.

steps.title: Maximum Y: spread the pages
steps.body: Put at least one accessed page in every 1024-page region, so that every inner page holds a valid entry. There are only 1024 regions and 2000 pages are enough to touch them all, so all 1024 inner pages are allocated: $Y = 1 + 1024 = 1025$. Hence $X + Y = 3 + 1025 = 1028$ (derivation: hierarchical page tables, sparse processes).

shortcut.body: Entries per page $= 2^{10}$. Minimum $1 + \lceil 2000/1024 \rceil = 3$; maximum $1 + \min(2000, 2^{10}) = 1025$; the sum is 1028.

traps.text: Giving every accessed page its own inner page makes $Y = 2001$ and $X + Y = 2004$. The directory has only 1024 entries, so at most 1024 inner pages can exist.
Leaving out the directory page in both counts gives $2 + 1024 = 1026$. The question counts pages across both levels, and the directory page was allocated at process creation.

recognize.clues: The question has an outer directory that always exists, inner pages allocated on demand, and asks for the minimum and maximum number of table pages when a fixed number of unique pages is touched.
recognize.contrast: A single-level table is allocated whole whatever is touched. Here the count depends on how sparse the accessed pages are, so a best case and a worst case differ.

check.body: Substitute the numbers. $X=1+\lceil 2000/1024\rceil=1+2=3$ and $Y=1+\min(2000,1024)=1025$. Then $Y\le 1+1024$ holds with equality, because 2000 touched pages are enough to reach all 1024 inner pages, and $X+Y=1028$.

questions.stem: Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of 2 KB. Assume that both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages 0, 1, 2, and 3 are stored in the page frames 1, 3, 2, and 0, respectively. The physical address (in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address 2500 (in decimal format) is ________

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body: A virtual address is the address a program uses; a physical address names a location in main memory. Both count bytes from 0. Virtual memory is cut into pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, here 2 KB. A virtual address splits into a page number, the address divided by the page size, and an offset, the remainder, which is the byte's position inside the page. The page table says which frame holds each page. The rule: translation replaces the page number by its frame number and keeps the offset, so physical address = frame number × page size + offset.

steps.title: Split the virtual address
steps.body: With pages of $2\text{ KB} = 2048$ bytes, dividing 2500 by 2048 gives page 1 and offset 452 (derivation: address split and the size of a single-level page table).

steps.title: Replace the page number by the frame number
steps.body: Page 1 is stored in frame 3, and the offset does not change, so the physical address is $3 \times 2048 + 452 = 6144 + 452 = 6596$.

shortcut.body: Page $= \lfloor 2500/2048 \rfloor = 1$ and offset $= 452$; frame 3 gives $3 \times 2048 + 452 = 6596$. In binary the same step swaps the page bits 1 for the frame bits 11 in front of the 11-bit offset.

traps.text: Reading the list as frames 0, 1, 2, 3 holding pages 1, 3, 2, 0 puts page 1 in frame 0 and gives 452. The question lists the frames of pages 0, 1, 2 and 3, in that order.
Taking 2 KB as 2000 bytes gives page 1, offset 500 and the address 6500.
Dropping the offset gives 6144, which is only the start of frame 3.

recognize.clues: A fixed page size, an explicit page-to-frame list and one virtual address to convert point to the plain split into page number and offset, with no table size or TLB involved.
recognize.contrast: Do not reach for the page-table-size formulas: nothing here asks how large the table is or how many bits each field has, only where one given byte lands.

check.body: Run it backwards. Subtract the frame start from the physical address to recover the offset, then divide the frame number back to its page and rebuild the virtual address. The offset must be the same on both sides and smaller than the page size, and the physical address must lie inside the frame you chose.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two-dimensional array $D$ in the C programming language, which is stored in row-major order:

int D[128][128];

Demand paging is used for allocating memory and each physical page frame holds 512 elements of the array $D$. The Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement policy is used by the operating system. A total of 30 physical page frames are allocated to a process which executes the following code snippet:

The number of page faults generated during the execution of this code snippet is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The 32 pages of D with four rows each, and the 30-frame LRU queue at the end of column 0 and after the first two accesses of column 1, showing that each page is evicted just before it is needed again: 32 faults per column, 4096 in all.

steps.title: The terms and the one rule
steps.body:
Row-major order means the array is laid out in memory one whole row after another, so element $D[r][c]$ sits at position $128r + c$ counted in elements. Memory is cut into pages, and one page frame holds one page, here 512 elements. Demand paging loads a page only when the program first touches it, and a touch of a page that is not in one of the process's frames is a page fault. When all frames are full, LRU (least recently used) throws out the page whose last touch is oldest.
The rule that decides this question: a loop faults on a page every time the page is missing from memory at the moment the loop touches it. So we must find which pages the loop touches, in which order, and whether the 30 frames can keep a page until its next visit.

steps.title: Which page holds which element
steps.body: A page holds 512 elements and a row has 128, so one page holds $512/128 = 4$ whole rows. Position $128j + i$ with $0 \le i < 128$ lies in page $\lfloor (128j + i)/512 \rfloor = \lfloor j/4 \rfloor$: the column number $i$ never changes the page, only the row number $j$ does. The array has $128/4 = 32$ pages, $P_0$ to $P_{31}$.

steps.title: One pass of the inner loop
steps.body: The inner loop changes $j$ from 0 to 127 while $i$ stays fixed, so it walks down a column: rows 0 to 3 are all in $P_0$ (four touches), rows 4 to 7 in $P_1$, and so on up to $P_{31}$. Inside a run of four touches of the same page, only the first can fault; the other three find the page already loaded. So one column visits the pages $P_0, P_1, \dots, P_{31}$ in this order, and each column makes at most 32 faults.

steps.title: LRU with 30 frames on a cycle of 32 pages
steps.body:
Column 0: every page is new, so all 32 touches fault. The first 30 faults fill the frames with $P_0$ to $P_{29}$; the fault on $P_{30}$ evicts the oldest, $P_0$; the fault on $P_{31}$ evicts $P_1$. Frames now hold $P_2$ to $P_{31}$.
Column 1 starts with $P_0$, which was just evicted: fault, and the oldest page $P_2$ is thrown out. Next $P_1$: fault, and $P_3$ is thrown out. In general the page the loop asks for next is always the one LRU discarded about 30 touches ago, so no page is ever found in memory when its next column begins. Every column therefore costs exactly 32 faults.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: There are 128 columns, each with 32 faults. The result matches the key.

shortcut.body: Pages per column: $512$ elements per page is 4 rows, so a column touches $128/4 = 32$ pages in the same order every time. A cyclic sweep over more pages (32) than frames (30) is the worst case for LRU, because the page about to be reused is always the one just evicted, so every page change faults: $128 \times 32 = 4096$. This shortcut needs the cycle to be longer than the frame count; with 32 or more frames the answer would be just 32. It also holds for FIFO here.

traps.text: Answering 16384, one fault per access ($128 \times 128$). The chapter's column-wise rule of $R \times C$ faults needs a row to fill a page; here a page holds 4 rows, so three of every four consecutive touches hit.

Answering 32. That is the number of faults when the loop runs row by row (each page visited once) or when 32 or more frames are available. With 30 frames and column order the pages are reused, but too late.
Counting only the overflow, $128 \times (32 - 30) = 256$. LRU does not keep 30 of the 32 pages for reuse: on a cyclic sweep it keeps the 30 that will be needed last and discards the one needed first.

recognize.clues: A column-wise walk over a row-major array, a fixed number of frames and LRU: the page reference order repeats each outer iteration and the question counts faults.
recognize.contrast: Plain demand paging counts first-touch faults only; here the frames are fewer than the cycle of pages, so replacement decides the count, not first touches.

check.body: Test the opposite case. With 32 or more frames every page of a column stays resident, so only the first column faults and the total is just the number of pages, 32. Giving the process fewer frames than the cycle length breaks that, which is why the count jumps to a fault on every page change.

questions.stem:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level tree-structured page tables with $L$ levels for virtual to physical address translation. The page size is 4 KB ($1\text{ KB} = 1024$ B) and a page table entry at any of the levels occupies 8 bytes.

The value of $L$ is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The 57-bit virtual address cut into a 12-bit page offset and five 9-bit level indexes, so five levels.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
A virtual address is a page number followed by an offset inside the page. A page table maps the page number to a frame. When the page number is too long for one table, it is cut into several indexes: the first index picks an entry in the top table, that entry points to a table of the next level, and so on; the last level gives the frame. In a tree-structured table every table is stored in exactly one page, so one table holds $\text{page size} / \text{entry size}$ entries and each level consumes $\log_2$ of that many bits.
The rule: $L = \lceil \text{page-number bits} / \text{bits per level} \rceil$, and the page-number bits are the address bits minus the offset bits.

steps.title: Offset and page-number bits
steps.body: A 4 KB page is $2^{12}$ bytes, so the offset takes 12 bits. The remaining $57 - 12 = 45$ bits are the page number.

steps.title: Bits resolved at one level
steps.body: One table fills one page: $4096 / 8 = 512 = 2^9$ entries. Nine index bits select one of 512 entries, so each level resolves 9 bits.

steps.title: Number of levels
steps.body: 45 bits divided by 9 bits per level is exactly 5, so every level's table fills a page with no waste. With 4 levels of 9 bits only 36 bits are covered; to cover all 45 the top table would need $45 - 27 = 18$ index bits, that is $2^{18}$ entries of 8 bytes (2 MB), far more than one page. So $L = 5$.

shortcut.body: Per level: $\log_2(4096/8) = 9$. Page number: $57 - 12 = 45$. $45/9 = 5$. Whenever the page-number bits are not a multiple of the per-level bits, round up and let the top table be smaller.

traps.text: Forgetting the offset: $57/9 = 6.3$, rounded up to 7. The 12 offset bits are never translated, so they are not split across levels.
Counting the offset as a level, or dividing 45 by 8 and rounding up: both give 6. The data page is the target of the last table, not another table.
Using 4 levels because 48-bit machines have 4. A 48-bit address has 36 page-number bits ($4 \times 9$); 57 bits needs a fifth level.
Reading the entry as 4 bytes gives 10 bits per level and also $\lceil 45/10 \rceil = 5$, but that is luck and the question says 8 bytes.

recognize.clues: A wide virtual address, a stated page size and entry size, and an unknown number of levels L point to splitting the page number over page-sized tables.
recognize.contrast: This is not the page-table-size calculation: the unknown is the depth of the tree, which comes from dividing bit counts, not from multiplying entries by entry size.

check.body: Multiply back. If L levels of the per-level bits are used, the covered bits are L times the per-level count, and that must reach the page-number width. One level fewer must fall short; if it does not, the depth is too large. Add the offset bits to the covered bits and compare with the address width.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The TLB performs an associative search in parallel on all its valid entries using page number of incoming virtual address.
If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit, but the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in the main memory.
The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.
In a system that uses hashed page tables, if two distinct virtual addresses V1 and V2 map to the same value while hashing, then the memory access time of these addresses will not be the same.

solutionDiagram.alt: A hashed page table bucket whose chain holds V1 then V2, so V1 costs one read and V2 two; below it an inverted table of frames scanned from frame 0, whose cost depends on where the match is.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small hardware memory that remembers recent page-number to frame-number translations. It is built as an associative memory: the incoming page number is compared with every entry at the same time. The cache is a different, small, fast memory that holds recently used words of main memory. A TLB entry exists only for a page that is in main memory.
An inverted page table has one entry per physical frame, holding (process id, page number); to translate, the system must find the entry whose pair matches, and the frame number is that entry's position. A hashed page table hashes the page number to a bucket and follows a chain of entries in that bucket.
To find the FALSE statement, test each one against these facts. A lookup that has to search takes longer when the match is further along.

steps.title: Statements A and B are true
steps.body: A: associative lookup compares the page number against all valid TLB entries in parallel, which is why the TLB is fast. B: a TLB entry is removed when its page leaves memory, so a TLB hit means the page is resident in main memory. A following cache miss only means the word is not in the cache; it is fetched from main memory, where its page is. So the word is always in main memory.

steps.title: Statement D is true
steps.body: If V1 and V2 hash to the same bucket, both are entries in one chain. They cannot sit in the same position, so one is found after reading fewer chain elements than the other, and their access times differ.

steps.title: Statement C is false
steps.body: An inverted table must be searched for the (process id, page) pair. By linear scan, a match in frame 0 costs one read and a match in frame $n-1$ costs $n$ reads; with a hash on top, the cost is the length of the chain walked. Either way the time depends on the address, so "always same for all incoming virtual addresses" is false. The answer is C.

shortcut.body: Look for the absolute claim that a search structure behaves uniformly. Anything that is searched (scan or hash chain) costs different amounts for different keys, so C ("always same") fails at once; A and B are standard facts about the TLB, and D is the collision-chain fact. The word "always" is only a hint: B also has "always" and is true, so check the reason.

traps.text: Thinking the TLB checks entries one by one. It is associative hardware that compares all valid entries in parallel; A is true.
Thinking a TLB hit followed by a cache miss could mean the page is on disk. A TLB entry maps only resident pages, so the page is in main memory; B is true.

Reading D as false because hashing "gives constant time". Constant time holds only on average without collisions; once V1 and V2 collide, they sit at different places in the chain and cost different reads.

recognize.clues: Statements about inverted and hashed page tables, with a word like "always" about access time, ask how a lookup is performed and whether its cost varies.
recognize.contrast: A normal page table is indexed directly by page number and costs the same for every address; the inverted and hashed tables must search, which is what separates them.

check.body: Build a tiny counter-example for each suspect statement. For an inverted table of four frames, put one address in the first entry and another in the last and count the reads each needs. If the counts differ, the claim of equal time cannot hold for that structure.

questions.stem:
Consider a demand paging system with four page frames (initially empty) and LRU page replacement policy. For the following page reference string

7, 2, 7, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4, 6, 7, 7, 1, 5, 6, 1

the page fault rate, defined as the ratio of number of page faults to the number of memory accesses (rounded off to one decimal place) is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: LRU with four frames over the 15 references: the frame contents after every reference from least to most recently used, with F or H below each, giving 9 faults and 6 hits.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
Memory is divided into frames; each frame holds one page of the program. A reference to a page that is in a frame is a hit. A reference to a page that is not in any frame is a page fault: the page must be loaded. While a frame is empty it is simply filled; once all 4 are full, the policy chooses a victim. LRU (least recently used) chooses the page whose last reference is oldest, so we keep the frames ordered from least to most recently used: a hit moves the page to the most-recent end, a fault adds the new page there and removes from the old end if the frames are full.
The fault rate is faults divided by references, here out of 15.

steps.title: References 1 to 7: the frames fill up
steps.body:
Order below is least recent first.
1. 7: fault, [7]
2. 2: fault, [7, 2]
3. 7: hit, [2, 7]
4. 3: fault, [2, 7, 3]
5. 2: hit, [7, 3, 2]
6. 5: fault, [7, 3, 2, 5] (all 4 frames full)
7. 3: hit, [7, 2, 5, 3]
So far 4 faults and 3 hits.

steps.title: References 8 to 15: replacements
steps.body:
8. 4: fault, evict 7 (oldest), [2, 5, 3, 4]
9. 6: fault, evict 2, [5, 3, 4, 6]
10. 7: fault, evict 5, [3, 4, 6, 7]
11. 7: hit, [3, 4, 6, 7]
12. 1: fault, evict 3, [4, 6, 7, 1]
13. 5: fault, evict 4, [6, 7, 1, 5]
14. 6: hit, [7, 1, 5, 6]
15. 1: hit, [7, 5, 6, 1]
These eight references add 5 faults and 3 hits.

steps.title: Fault rate
steps.body: Total: 9 faults and 6 hits in 15 references. The rate is $9/15 = 0.6$, which is already one decimal place.

shortcut.body: Under LRU with $f$ frames, a reference hits exactly when fewer than $f$ distinct other pages were used since its previous use. Here $f = 4$, so a hit needs at most 3 distinct pages in between. Check the repeats only: ref 3 (7): {2}, hit. Ref 5 (2): {7, 3}, hit. Ref 7 (3): {2, 5}, hit. Ref 10 (7): {3, 2, 5, 4, 6} is 5 pages, fault. Ref 11 (7): none, hit. Ref 14 (6): {7, 1, 5} is 3, hit. Ref 15 (1): {5, 6}, hit. That is 6 hits and 9 faults, $9/15 = 0.6$. Safe for LRU only; it does not apply to FIFO.

traps.text: Answering 0.4, the hit ratio $6/15$, instead of the fault rate.

Answering 0.5, the optimal policy's result ($7$ faults, $7/15 = 0.47$). Evicting the page used farthest in the future is OPT, not LRU. Seven is also the number of distinct pages, the lower bound on faults for any policy.
Answering 9, the number of faults, instead of the rate. (FIFO also gives 9 faults on this string, so the number alone does not prove LRU was applied correctly.)

recognize.clues: A given reference string, a fixed frame count, an explicit LRU policy and a fault rate: simulate the string reference by reference.
recognize.contrast: FIFO also takes a reference string and frame count, but it evicts by arrival order; telling them apart means asking whether a hit changes the eviction order, which it does under LRU.

check.body: Check by the stack-distance test. Under LRU with four frames, a reference hits exactly when fewer than four distinct other pages were used since its previous use. Apply that to each repeated reference and count the hits independently; hits plus faults must equal the number of references.

questions.stem:
Consider a three-level page table to translate a 39-bit virtual address to a physical address as shown below.

The page size is 4KB ($1\text{KB} = 2^{10}$ bytes) and page table entry size at every level is 8 bytes. A process $P$ is currently using 2GB ($1\text{GB} = 2^{30}$ bytes) virtual memory which is mapped to 2GB of physical memory. The minimum amount of memory required for the page table of $P$ across all levels is ________ KB.
questions.figure: The 39-bit virtual address is divided into four fields, left to right: Level 1 offset (9 bits), Level 2 offset (9 bits), Level 3 offset (9 bits) and Page offset (12 bits).

diagram.alt: The 39-bit virtual address as four boxes from left to right: Level 1 offset 9 bits, Level 2 offset 9 bits, Level 3 offset 9 bits, Page offset 12 bits.

solutionDiagram.alt: Tree of tables for 2 GB: one level-1 table with two entries in use, two level-2 tables with all 512 entries in use, and 512 level-3 tables below each, 1027 tables of 4 KB in all.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
A multi-level page table is a tree of tables. The top (level 1) table is indexed by the first 9 address bits; each of its entries points to a level-2 table, indexed by the next 9 bits; each of those entries points to a level-3 table, indexed by the next 9 bits, whose entries hold frame numbers. The last 12 bits are the offset inside a 4 KB page and are not translated.
A table with $2^9 = 512$ entries of 8 bytes is $512 \times 8 = 4096$ bytes: exactly one page, 4 KB. The tree is built on demand, so a table is allocated only if some entry below it is in use. The rule: count the tables needed at each level from the bottom up, then multiply by 4 KB. The minimum is reached when the 2 GB is one contiguous, aligned block, so it touches as few tables as possible.

steps.title: Pages in use
steps.body: A page is 4 KB, so 2 GB is $2^{31}/2^{12} = 2^{19} = 524288$ pages. Each used page needs one entry in a level-3 table. (The mapping to 2 GB of physical memory does not add tables; it only says the pages are really there.)

steps.title: Tables at each level, bottom up
steps.body: Level 3: one table holds 512 entries, so $2^{19}/2^{9} = 2^{10} = 1024$ tables. Level 2: each of those 1024 tables needs one entry in a level-2 table, and one level-2 table holds 512, so $1024/512 = 2$ tables. Level 1: the 2 level-2 tables need 2 entries, which fit in one level-1 table, so 1 table.

steps.title: Total memory
steps.body: Tables: $1 + 2 + 1024 = 1027$, each 4 KB, so $1027 \times 4 = 4108$ KB. This matches the key.

shortcut.body: Pages $= 2^{19}$. Level-3 tables $= 2^{19}/2^9 = 1024$ (4096 KB). Level 2 needs 2, level 1 needs 1: three more tables, 12 KB. $4096 + 8 + 4 = 4108$. Every table is exactly one page here, so counting tables is counting pages of memory. This works because the 2 GB is contiguous; scattered use would need more tables.

traps.text: Answering 4096: that is the level-3 tables alone, which is also the size of one flat table with $2^{19}$ entries of 8 bytes. The upper levels are extra.
Answering 4104 by adding the level-2 tables but forgetting the single level-1 table, or 4100 by forgetting level 2.
Allocating every table the address space could ever need ($1 + 512 + 512^2$ tables, 1050628 KB). Inner tables exist only for regions in use, which is the whole point of the hierarchy.

recognize.clues: A three-level table with fields of equal width, a process using a fixed amount of memory, and the words "minimum amount of memory required" for the tables.
recognize.contrast: Single-level table size is entries times entry size for the whole address space; here only the part that is in use is allocated, which is why the tree is smaller than a flat table.

check.body: Cross-check with the top-down capacity. A level-3 table maps 512 pages, a level-2 table maps 512 of those, and the top table maps 512 of those. Verify that the tables counted at each level can actually map the pages in use, and that one fewer table at any level would leave some page unmapped.

questions.stem: Assume that in a certain computer, the virtual addresses are 64 bits long and the physical addresses are 48 bits long. The memory is word addressible. The page size is 8 kB and the word size is 4 bytes. The Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) in the address translation path has 128 valid entries. At most how many distinct virtual addresses can be translated without any TLB miss?

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
Virtual memory splits a process's address space into equal blocks called pages; the page table maps each page to a frame of physical memory. Reading the page table costs an extra memory access, so the Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB), a small fast cache, keeps recently used page-to-frame translations, one per entry. A TLB hit means the page of the address has an entry, so the address is translated at once. A TLB miss means no entry covers its page, and the page table must be read. A memory is word addressable when each address names one word (here 4 bytes), not one byte, so consecutive addresses are 4 bytes apart.
The rule: one entry translates every address inside its page, so the addresses translatable without a miss are the number of entries times the addresses per page, and with word addressing the addresses per page are page size divided by word size.

steps.title: Addresses covered by one entry
steps.body: Every address inside a cached page translates without a miss. Each address names a 4-byte word, so an 8 kB page holds $8192/4 = 2048 = 2^{11}$ addresses.

steps.title: All 128 entries
steps.body: 128 valid entries hold 128 different pages, so at most $2^7 \times 2^{11} = 2^{18}$ addresses translate without a miss, which is $256 \times 2^{10}$: option B. The 64-bit and 48-bit widths play no part; they would size the page and frame numbers stored in each entry.

shortcut.body: TLB coverage = entries × addresses per page. With word addressing, divide the page size by the word size first: $2^7 \times 2^{13} / 2^2 = 2^{18}$.

traps.text: Multiplying by the word size instead of dividing gives $128 \times 8\text{ kB} \times 4 = 4 \times 2^{20}$. A word address covers four bytes, so there are fewer addresses than bytes.

$8 \times 2^{20}$ is the byte count $2^{20}$ times 8, as if every bit had an address. Byte addressing alone gives $128 \times 8\text{ kB} = 2^{20}$, which is not offered; that is the cue to divide by the word size.

recognize.clues: The question asks how many distinct virtual addresses translate with no TLB miss, giving the number of valid entries, the page size and the word size.
recognize.contrast: This is TLB reach, not effective access time: no hit ratio or timing is given, only coverage counted in addresses rather than bytes.

check.body: Count in bytes and convert. The 128 pages cover 128 times 8 KB bytes of virtual space in total. Dividing that byte count by the 4 bytes per word must give the same number of addresses as the page-wise count. The 64-bit and 48-bit widths do not enter either route.

questions.stem:
Consider a process executing on an operating system that uses demand paging. The average time for a memory access in the system is M units if the corresponding memory page is available in memory, and D units if the memory access causes a page fault. It has been experimentally measured that the average time taken for a memory access in the process is X units.

Which one of the following is the correct expression for the page fault rate experienced by the process?

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
In demand paging a page is brought into memory only when the process first touches it. A page fault happens when an access names a page that is not in memory; the operating system then loads it from disk, which makes that access far slower. The page-fault rate is the fraction of all memory accesses that fault, a number between 0 and 1. So every access is one of two kinds: it finds its page in memory and takes $M$ units, or it faults and takes $D$ units.
The rule: the average time of a mix of two kinds of event is the sum of each time weighted by the fraction of accesses of that kind. This is the effective-access-time formula.

steps.title: Average over the two cases
steps.body: Let $p$ be the page-fault rate. An access takes $M$ with probability $1 - p$ and $D$ with probability $p$, and the measured average is $X$.

steps.title: Solve for the rate
steps.body: Subtract $M$ and divide by $D - M$: $p = (X - M)/(D - M)$, option B. As a check, $X = M$ gives $p = 0$ and $X = D$ gives $p = 1$.

shortcut.body: Test the boundaries. If no access faults, $X = M$ and the rate must be 0; if every access faults, $X = D$ and the rate must be 1. Only (B) gives both: (A) divides by zero at $X = M$, (C) gives 1 there, and (D) divides by zero at $X = D$.

traps.text: (A) is the reciprocal $1/p$; it exceeds 1 whenever $X < D$, so it cannot be a rate.
(C) equals $1 - p$, the fraction of accesses that find the page in memory.
(D) equals $p/(1 - p)$, faults per access that does not fault. It is close to $p$ only when $p$ is tiny, and it is not the rate.

recognize.clues: Two access times, one for a page in memory and one for a page fault, a measured average, and a request for the page fault rate as an expression.
recognize.contrast: The TLB formula has a similar weighted average, but it weighs hit and miss paths by their added lookups; here the two times are given directly as M and D.

check.body: Substitute numbers. Take M = 40, D = 900 and a fault rate of 0.02, which gives an average of 57.2. Plug that average into your expression and the 0.02 must come back. Also test the boundary cases where the average equals M and where it equals D.

questions.stem: In the context of operating systems, which of the following statements is/are correct with respect to paging?
options: Paging helps solve the issue of external fragmentation.
Page size has no impact on internal fragmentation.
Paging incurs memory overheads.
Multi-level paging is necessary to support pages of different sizes.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
Paging cuts physical memory into equal blocks called frames and a process's address space into pages of the same size. A page may sit in any frame, and the page table, kept in main memory, records which frame holds which page. Fragmentation is memory that is wasted. External fragmentation means the free memory is enough in total but is split into separate holes, none large enough for a request that must be one contiguous block. Internal fragmentation means space inside a block that was handed out but is not used, for example the unused tail of a process's last page. Overhead is memory spent on bookkeeping instead of on the program's own data. Multi-level paging stores the page table as a tree of small tables instead of one long table.
The rule: judge each statement by what the mechanism does. A request is served in whole units of one fixed size, placed anywhere. So the only waste is inside the last unit, which depends on the unit size, and the page tables themselves take space.

steps.title: A is correct, B is not
steps.body:
A: a process needs only as many free frames as it has pages, and the frames need not be next to each other. Four separate 2 KB holes (8 KB free) cannot hold a contiguous 5 KB request, but with 2 KB frames the same memory serves a 3-page process. So no free frame is ever unusable and paging removes external fragmentation.
B: a process of 10001 bytes needs 3 pages of 4096 bytes and wastes $3 \times 4096 - 10001 = 2287$ bytes in the last page, but with 1024-byte pages it needs 10 pages and wastes only $10 \times 1024 - 10001 = 239$ bytes. The waste in the last page is between 0 and one page, about half a page on average, so a larger page size means more internal fragmentation. A simulation over 100000 random process sizes gave an average waste of 512, 2053 and 8301 bytes for pages of 1 KB, 4 KB and 16 KB, close to half the page size.

steps.title: C is correct, D is not
steps.body:
C: the page table takes memory, and with a 32-bit address, 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries one flat table has $2^{20}$ entries, which is 4 MB for every process, besides the internal fragmentation of B. So paging does cost memory.
D: multi-level paging exists to make the page table smaller for a sparse address space: a process using 2 MB of contiguous memory (512 pages) needs a 4 MB flat table but only 8 KB in two levels (one directory page and one inner page). It is a way to store the table, not a requirement for supporting several page sizes; a single-level table can carry a page-size field in each entry. So D is not necessary. The correct statements are A and C.

shortcut.body: Test the absolute words first. B says "no impact" and D says "necessary": both are strong claims, and one counter-case kills each (a bigger page wastes more in the last page; a flat table with a size field also works). A and C are the textbook facts: no external fragmentation, and page tables cost memory. About one minute.

traps.text: B comes from remembering that paging has no external fragmentation and stretching it to "no fragmentation". The last page of a process is partly empty, and a bigger page leaves more of it empty.

D confuses the purpose of multi-level tables. They shrink the page table of a sparse address space. Different page sizes (huge pages) are an extra feature that is not needed for paging to work, so "necessary" is wrong.
Leaving A out because paging still has internal fragmentation. The statement is only about external fragmentation, and paging does remove that.
Leaving C out because paging "saves" memory by avoiding holes. The page tables, and the half-empty last page of each process, are real memory overhead.

recognize.clues: A "which statements are correct" list about paging with absolute wording ("no impact", "necessary") next to two plain textbook claims about fragmentation and overhead.
recognize.contrast: os-memory-management.multi-level-page-tables is the look-alike in the last option: it shrinks the page table of a sparse address space and has nothing to do with supporting several page sizes.

check.body: Take a 5000-byte process. With 2 KB pages it needs 3 pages and wastes $3 \times 2048 - 5000 = 1144$ bytes; with 8 KB pages it needs 1 page and wastes $8192 - 5000 = 3192$ bytes. The waste grew with the page size, so "no impact" fails. For the table, a 32-bit space with 8 KB pages has $2^{19}$ entries, half as many as with 4 KB pages, so the table is a real cost that shrinks as pages grow.

questions.stem: Consider allocation of memory to a new process. Assume that none of the existing holes in the memory will exactly fit the process's memory requirement. Hence, a new hole of smaller size will be created if allocation is made in any of the existing holes. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The hole created by first fit is always larger than the hole created by next fit.
The hole created by worst fit is always larger than the hole created by first fit.
The hole created by best fit is never larger than the hole created by first fit.
The hole created by next fit is never larger than the hole created by best fit.

solutionDiagram.alt: A 15 KB request against holes of 40, 20, 60 and 25 KB: first fit uses the 40 KB hole and leaves 25, best fit uses the 20 KB hole and leaves 5, worst fit uses the 60 KB hole and leaves 45, and next fit scanning from the third hole also leaves 45.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
In contiguous allocation a process gets one block of memory. A hole is a free block between allocated blocks, and a hole fits a request when it is at least as large as the request. Placing the request in a hole leaves a smaller hole, the remainder: hole size minus request size. Four policies choose among the holes that fit. First fit takes the first fitting hole, scanning from the start of memory. Next fit is the same but starts scanning where the previous search stopped, wrapping around at the end. Best fit takes the smallest fitting hole. Worst fit takes the largest.
The rule: the request is the same in all four cases, so comparing the holes created is the same as comparing the chosen holes. Every policy picks one of the fitting holes, best fit picks the minimum and worst fit the maximum, and first and next fit pick whichever fitting hole their scan meets first. The words "always" and "never" mean the statement must hold for every list of holes and every scan start, so a single counterexample makes it false.

steps.title: One example with all four policies
steps.body: Holes in memory order: H1 = 40, H2 = 20, H3 = 60, H4 = 25 KB. A request of 15 KB fits every hole and matches none exactly. First fit takes H1 and leaves 25. Best fit takes H2, the smallest, and leaves 5. Worst fit takes H3, the largest, and leaves 45. Next fit depends on where its scan starts: from H1 it leaves 25, from H2 it leaves 5, from H3 it leaves 45, and from H4 it leaves 10. The diagram shows these remainders.

steps.title: A, B and D each have a counterexample
steps.body:
A says first fit is always larger than next fit. If the next-fit scan starts at H1, both take H1 and leave 25, which is equal, not larger. With a single hole all four policies are identical, so "always larger" fails at once.
B says worst fit is always larger than first fit. For holes 60, 20 and a request of 15, first fit takes the 60 KB hole, which is also the largest, so both leave 45.
D says next fit is never larger than best fit. In the example, next fit started at H3 leaves 45 and best fit leaves 5, so next fit is larger. All three are false.

steps.title: C holds for every list of holes
steps.body: Best fit chooses the smallest fitting hole, so its remainder is the smallest of all possible remainders. First fit chooses some fitting hole, so its remainder is at least best fit's. Hence the hole created by best fit is never larger than the one created by first fit, with equality when first fit happens to meet the smallest fitting hole. The exhaustive check of all hole lists with up to 5 holes of sizes 1 to 8, every request without an exact fit and every next-fit start (591,780 cases) found no violation of C and counterexamples to A, B and D. The answer is C.

shortcut.body: Best fit is the minimum over the fitting holes, so no other policy can leave a smaller hole. That makes "best fit ... never larger than" any other policy true, and D, which puts best fit on the wrong side, false. A and B say "always larger", which fails when both policies pick the same hole, for instance with a single hole. About one minute. The shortcut is unsafe if a statement says "smaller" or "larger" without the always or never wording.

traps.text: A treats next fit as a cleverer first fit. Both are position-driven choices, and next fit may land on the very hole first fit uses (equal remainders) or on a bigger one.
B is tempting because worst fit takes the largest hole. First fit may already meet that same hole, giving equal remainders, so worst fit is not always larger.
D assumes next fit is close to best fit. Its scan start is arbitrary, so it may pick a big hole and leave a remainder far larger than best fit's smallest one.
Reading "always larger" as "larger or equal" turns A and B into plausible statements. The wording is strict, and equality already breaks them.

recognize.clues: Four statements comparing the size of the hole left by first, next, best and worst fit, with "always" and "never", and a request that fits no hole exactly.

questions.stem: Consider a paging system that uses 1-level page table residing in main memory and a TLB for address translation. Each main memory access takes 100 ns and TLB lookup takes 20 ns. Each page transfer to/from the disk takes 5000 ns. Assume that the TLB hit ratio is 95%, page fault rate is 10%. Assume that for 20% of the total page faults, a dirty page has to be written back to disk before the required page is read in from disk. TLB update time is negligible. The average memory access time in ns (round off to 1 decimal places) is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Probability tree for one reference: TLB hit 0.95 costs 120 ns, TLB miss 0.05 then either page valid 0.90 at 220 ns or page fault 0.10 at 6220 ns; weighted contributions 114.0, 9.9 and 31.1 add to 155.0 ns.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
A page table maps a page number to a frame. A one-level table in main memory costs one extra memory access for every translation that is not already cached. The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small fast table of recent translations. A hit means the translation is there, a miss means it is not, and the hit ratio is the fraction of references that hit. A page fault happens when the page-table entry says the page is not in main memory. The OS then reads the page from disk, taking the page-transfer time. If the frame it reuses holds a dirty page, one modified since it was loaded, that page is first written back to disk, so the service takes two transfers instead of one. The average access time is the probability-weighted cost of the disjoint cases a reference can end in.
The rule: split each reference into disjoint cases, find the cost of each, and weight by the probabilities. A TLB entry exists only for a page that is in memory, so a TLB hit cannot fault. A fault is found only when the page-table entry is read, which happens only after a miss, so the 10% fault rate is a fraction of the TLB misses.

steps.title: Cost of each case without a fault
steps.body: Every reference starts with the 20 ns TLB lookup. On a hit the data read follows: $20 + 100 = 120$ ns. On a miss the page table is read from memory, 100 ns, and then the data, 100 ns: $20 + 100 + 100 = 220$ ns.

steps.title: Mean fault service time
steps.body: Reading the missing page takes 5000 ns. For 20% of the faults a dirty page is written back first, which makes 10000 ns. The mean service time is $0.8 \times 5000 + 0.2 \times 10000 = 6000$ ns. A faulting reference follows the miss path, 220 ns, plus this service time, since after the page is loaded the data is read as in an ordinary miss: $220 + 6000 = 6220$ ns.

steps.title: Weight the three cases
steps.body: The cases are: hit with probability 0.95, miss with a valid page with probability $0.05 \times 0.9$, and miss with a page fault with probability $0.05 \times 0.1$. The weighted sum is 155.0 ns, which lies in the official range 154.5 to 155.5. A simulation of 4 million references averaged 154.9 ns.

shortcut.body: Without faults the average is $0.95 \times 120 + 0.05 \times 220 = 125$ ns. Faults happen to $0.05 \times 0.1 = 0.005$ of the references, each adding $0.8 \times 5000 + 0.2 \times 10000 = 6000$ ns: $125 + 0.005 \times 6000 = 155$. The convention that a fault costs $20 + 100 + 6000$ (service, with no further data read) gives 154.5, which the key range also accepts. About three minutes.

traps.text: Applying the 10% fault rate to every reference, including TLB hits, gives $125 + 0.1 \times 6000 = 725$ ns. A TLB hit means the page is already in memory, so only a miss can fault.

Forgetting the write-back and using 5000 ns as the service time gives $125 + 0.005 \times 5000 = 150$ ns; treating every fault as dirty (10000 ns) gives 175 ns. Only 20% of the faults pay for two transfers.
Dropping the 20 ns lookup from every reference gives 135 ns. The TLB is consulted on every reference, hit or miss.

recognize.clues: A TLB hit ratio, memory and TLB times, a one-level page table in memory, a page fault rate, and a fraction of faults needing a write-back, with a request for an average time.
recognize.contrast: os-memory-management.demand-paging has a similar weighted average of hit and fault times, but it has no TLB layer; here the fault probability is conditioned on a TLB miss.

check.body: Check by bounding. With no faults the average is $0.95 \times 120 + 0.05 \times 220 = 125$ ns, and the average must exceed that. Faults reach only 0.5% of references, each adding 6000 ns of mean service, so the extra is about $0.005 \times 6000 = 30$ ns. Treating the fault rate as applying to every reference would add 600 ns instead, far above the stated range, which shows the conditioning matters.

hints.text: Which sequence of events can a single reference go through, and which of those can end in a page fault?
Average access time is the probability-weighted cost of disjoint cases: a TLB hit, a TLB miss with the page in memory, and a miss that faults.
A page that is in the TLB is in memory, so only a TLB miss can fault. The fault rate therefore applies to the misses, not to every reference.
Every reference pays the TLB lookup. A miss adds a page-table read and the data read from memory. A fault adds the disk service time on top, which averages over clean and dirty replacements.
Weight the clean and the dirty replacements by 0.8 and 0.2. A dirty one costs a write plus a read, a clean one only a read.

The average is $0.9(90) + 0.1(0.96)(170) + 0.1(0.04)(5170) = 81 + 16.32 + 20.68 = 118$ ns.

questions.stem:
Recall that Belady's anomaly is that the page-fault rate may increase as the number of allocated frames increases. Now, consider the following statements:

S1: Random page replacement algorithm (where a page chosen at random is replaced) suffers from Belady's anomaly
S2: LRU page replacement algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly

Which of the following is CORRECT?
options: S1 is true, S2 is true
S1 is true, S2 is false
S1 is false, S2 is true
S1 is false, S2 is false

solutionDiagram.alt: Page frames over time for one possible random-replacement run on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: with 3 frames there are 9 faults, with 4 frames there are 10, so more frames gave more faults.

steps.title: The terms and the rule
steps.body:
A frame holds one page of the process, and a page fault occurs when the referenced page is in no frame. A replacement algorithm picks the page to evict when all frames are full. Belady's anomaly means that for some reference string, giving the process more frames makes the number of page faults go up instead of down. To say an algorithm "suffers" from it, one string with one possible run is enough.
A stack algorithm is one whose set of resident pages with $f$ frames is always a subset of the set it would have with $f + 1$ frames on the same string, at every moment (the inclusion property). The rule: a stack algorithm can never show the anomaly, because every reference that hits with $f$ frames also hits with $f + 1$, so faults cannot rise; an algorithm without the inclusion property can.

steps.title: S2: LRU is a stack algorithm
steps.body: With $f$ frames LRU keeps the $f$ most recently used distinct pages. The $f$ most recent pages are always among the $f + 1$ most recent, so the resident set with $f$ frames is always inside the set with $f + 1$ frames. LRU therefore never faults more with more frames. A check over every string of length up to 9 on 5 pages, for 1 to 4 frames (7,324,215 comparisons), found the inclusion property and the fault-count ordering never violated. S2 is false.

steps.title: S1: a random choice can behave like FIFO
steps.body: Random replacement may evict any resident page. One of the outcomes is that it evicts the oldest page every time, which is exactly FIFO. On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, that run has 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 faults with 4 frames, as the diagram shows. After the 7th reference the 3-frame run holds {1, 2, 5} and the 4-frame run holds {2, 3, 4, 5}, so page 1 is in the smaller set only and inclusion fails. Trying every possible choice of victims, the 3-frame runs have 7 to 12 faults and the 4-frame runs have 6 to 10, so a 4-frame run can fault more than a 3-frame run. Random replacement suffers from the anomaly, so S1 is true.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: S1 is true and S2 is false, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Recall the classification. LRU and optimal are stack algorithms and never show the anomaly. FIFO and random (which can imitate FIFO) have no inclusion property, and FIFO on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. That fixes S1 true, S2 false in under a minute.

traps.text: Calling LRU anomalous because "every real algorithm can misbehave". Its inclusion property is a proof, not a tendency: the f most recent pages are always among the f + 1 most recent.
Taking LRU as the one that fails and random as safe, as if random behaviour averaged out. The statement only asks whether the anomaly can occur, and a random run that mimics FIFO shows it can.
Saying random cannot suffer because it has no fixed rule to blame. Belady's anomaly says the fault rate "may" increase; one possible run with more faults on more frames is enough.

recognize.clues: Two statements asking whether named replacement algorithms, one of them random, suffer from Belady's anomaly.
recognize.contrast: os-memory-management.replacement-policies covers how each algorithm picks a victim; the anomaly question is only about whether the resident set with fewer frames stays inside the set with more frames.

check.body: Run LRU on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 by hand: it faults 10 times with 3 frames and 8 times with 4 frames, so the count falls as the nesting argument predicts. A second boundary: with 1 frame every change of page faults, and with as many frames as distinct pages only the first use of each page faults, so no stack policy can rise between those ends.
